Vitamin C absorption does not appear to be abnormally low in healthy older people. However, the multiple pathologies asso-
ciated with old age (and with debility at any age) are associated with increased turnover of the vitamin. Older people with very low
levels of vitamin C are at higher risk of dying sooner than those with high levels, although short-term vitamin supplements generally
fail to reverse this increased risk. It thus appears that vitamin C status can act as a barometer of health as well as being a marker of
adequacy of vitamin C intake. Further research is needed to determine the key mechanisms that affect the rate of vitamin C turnover
and its control in different age groups and different metabolic states. Because frail older people are at high risk of developing pres-
sure sores and of needing surgery for a variety of ailments, there seems to be a potential public-health advantage in protecting
vitamin C stores, especially in this vulnerable older age group.
